messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Vinh Nguyen first learned the weight of helplessness forty years ago, watching his six-year-old daughter, Mei, fight for breath in a pediatric intensive care unit. A routine scraped knee had spiraled into septic shock, and for three agonizing weeks, Vinh stood vigil over a maze of tubes and ventilators. He remembered the sharp, clinical scent of antiseptic wipes clinging to the hallway, the sudden clatter of a nurse starting a new IV, and the way his chest would seize whenever the double doors swung open to reveal a pregnant woman in the waiting area. To Vinh, those moments were not distant memories of a crisis that had ended; they were visceral relivings. His body would flood with panic, his heart hammering against his ribs, a terrifying certainty that Mei was slipping away again. When he tried to tell his late wife what it felt like, the words dissolved into tangled silence, leaving him alone with the roaring dread. Over the decades, that terror calcified into quiet avoidance. He stopped attending family gatherings when a cousin expected a baby, convincing himself he was simply prioritizing work. He avoided doctors’ offices entirely, relying on his own rigid health monitoring until her passing left him without a buffer. Yet the loop tightened. When the antiseptic scent of a colleague’s hand sanitizer drifted across his open-plan office, or when the corporate wellness coordinator announced the annual blood draws, Vinh’s mind would instantly project backward. The past did not stay past; it rushed forward, coloring his present with a low, humming dread that made even routine security audits feel like navigating a minefield. His attention would snap to the smell of alcohol pads or the rustle of a maternity magazine, pulling his awareness backward until the boundaries of his office dissolved into the memory of the PICU. Now seventy-five, Vinh worked as a cybersecurity analyst for a municipal data firm, a role that demanded absolute stillness and hyper-vigilance. His daily environment became the stage for his quiet unraveling. The company’s annual occupational health screening was held in a repurposed conference room on the fourth floor, where the sterile air conditioning carried the unmistakable tang of hospital-grade disinfectant. When Vinh entered that room for his mandatory lipid panel, the moment the phlebotomist taped the tourniquet to his arm, his breathing fractured. The physical jolt was immediate and overwhelming—a cold sweat breaking across his back, a sudden inability to distinguish the office chair from the hospital bed. The terror that surged through him was so complete it felt like a new attack, not a reflection of an old one. That visceral alarm did not merely sit in the room; it acted as a lens, distorting everything around it. The cycle had long ago become self-sustaining. Every time his heart raced or guilt gnawed at his stomach for feeling afraid of the living, the memories sharpened, becoming clearer and more immediate, as though Mei’s hospital bed had never been cleared. The more present the past felt, the more potent the triggers became, and the more his body prepared for a disaster that had already passed. He had come to believe that his constant state of readiness was the only thing keeping the terror at bay, but the exhaustion was now absolute. What finally brought Vinh to a therapist’s office was not a single crisis, but a slow accumulation of isolation: he could no longer sit through his granddaughter’s recitals without calculating the distance to the nearest emergency room, and his hands would shake too violently to authenticate access codes. He did not want to be a prisoner of forty years ago, but he was terrified that without intervention, the fear would continue to dictate where he walked and what he allowed himself to feel. He hoped, quietly, that someone might help him untangle the wire between then and now, so he could finally rest.
